strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in video generation benchmarking by focusing on long-form and complex text-to-video generation with significantly longer prompts than existing benchmarks
Comprehensive multi-dimensional evaluation framework with 26 sub-dimensions organized across 5 main dimensions (SQ, TVA, TQ, CC, HERD), providing thorough coverage of video quality aspects

Novel HERD (Human Expectation Realization Degree) metric capturing high-level semantic attributes (emotional response, narrative flow, character development, visual style, themes) typically overlooked by existing metrics

Rigorous methodology including careful dataset curation (240 videos, 18 themes), sophisticated temporal consistency evaluation with intra/inter-event consistency measures, and event-level alignment using Hungarian algorithm

Thorough experimental evaluation of 9 representative methods with analysis of content type impact, prompt complexity effects, and metric correlations revealing clear performance gaps and method-specific strengths/weaknesses
Reproducibility commitment with detailed prompts, evaluation templates, JSON specifications, ethical statement, and promise to release code and data
Well-structured presentation with informative visualizations and case studies effectively demonstrating differences between generation methods
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty - primarily a benchmarking exercise relying heavily on existing tools (DOVER, Aesthetic Predictor V2, PySceneDetect) rather than proposing new evaluation approaches

HERD metric lacks validation: no inter-annotator agreement, no comparison against independent human evaluations, and no ablation studies on design choices; LLM-based randomness and polarity annotation may introduce biases

Critical metric reliability gap - no baseline human evaluation scores provided to validate correlation between proposed metrics and ground-truth human judgments, limiting confidence in metric soundness
Dataset limitations - 240 videos and 18 themes are modest; modest sample size and limited thematic coverage may not comprehensively capture the space of long-form complex video generation scenarios

Methodological concerns underaddressed: DOVER segmentation may introduce boundary artifacts; Aesthetic Predictor's arbitrary scale requires workaround; weak static quality correlation (Figure 3) questions its prominence; some metrics rely on simple comparisons
Limited actionable guidance - identifies performance gaps but provides minimal insight into how methods should be improved to address identified shortcomings
Reproducibility concerns - data not yet available, dependency on multiple external tools whose versions may change over time, LLM-based metrics vulnerable to model version drift

High complexity may limit adoption - 26 sub-dimensions, multiple mathematical formulations, dense presentation (30 pages), and dependency on several specialized tools create barriers for researchers extending or adopting the benchmark

strengths: Addresses a real gap in T2V benchmarking by focusing on long-form and complex text-to-video generation with more nuanced evaluation dimensions than existing benchmarks
Comprehensive multi-dimensional evaluation framework covering visual quality, alignment, temporal consistency, content clarity, and human expectations with well-motivated design
Systematic dataset construction with 240 videos manually curated across 18 themes incorporating real-world complexity (transitions, camera dynamics, event sequences)
Thorough empirical evaluation of 9 representative open-source LVG methods providing comparative performance insights
Well-organized presentation with clear figures, detailed appendices providing implementation details, and commit to releasing prompts and code
Analysis of how different prompt complexity types affect evaluation across dimensions offering some insights into method behavior
weaknesses: Critical flaw in HERD metric: Relies on LLMs scoring based on text descriptions of videos rather than analyzing actual video content—this is fundamentally circular and unvalidated. Claims about emotional response, narrative flow, and character development are inferred from LLM-generated text, not observed from video analysis

Complete absence of human evaluation studies: No validation that proposed metrics correlate with human judgment; no inter-rater reliability studies for subjective dimensions; no comparison of LLM-based scoring versus human scoring

Limited technical novelty: Primarily combines existing metrics (DOVER, CLIP) with LLM-based scoring via prompt engineering; no algorithmic innovations; event-level alignment using Hungarian algorithm is straightforward application of existing methods

Weak empirical insights and analysis: Results are reported but not deeply analyzed; paper states 'methods struggle with X' without explaining why or providing guidance for improvement; Section 4.4 claims dimension 'entanglement' without substantive explanation

Questionable validity of core metrics: Static quality evaluation on 10-second clips may miss temporal artifacts; aesthetic predictor trained on images not videos; content clarity relies on unvalidated LLM narrative assessment; no evidence these are better than simpler alternatives

Overclaimed scope: Average video length ~256 seconds (4 minutes) is moderate, not genuinely 'long-form'; dataset of 240 samples relatively small for modern benchmarks; limited to 18 themes with potential curation biases not documented

Insufficient analysis depth: Content type variation observed but not explained; semantic complexity finding deserves investigation but receives cursory treatment; missing comparison with recent benchmarks like VideoBench and EvalCrafter

Dataset and reproducibility concerns: HERD evaluation depends on non-deterministic LLM API calls; manual curation criteria not documented; full code not yet available; reliance on external LLM services limits reproducibility

strengths: Addresses genuine and important gap in video generation evaluation: existing benchmarks focus on short videos with simple prompts, while this benchmark systematically addresses long-form, complex text-to-video generation

Comprehensive and well-designed multi-dimensional evaluation framework with 5 major dimensions and 26 sub-dimensions, moving beyond traditional vision metrics to capture semantic coherence, temporal consistency, and narrative properties

Novel HERD (Human Expectation Realization Degree) metric that evaluates high-level semantic properties (emotional response, narrative flow, character development, themes) not captured by existing metrics
Rigorous methodological design including event-level alignment with temporal ordering penalties, intra/inter-event consistency metrics, and polarity-aware HERD question annotation to mitigate biases

Thorough experimental evaluation of 9 representative methods revealing systematic weaknesses in temporal consistency, fine-grained alignment, and narrative coherence, with useful analysis of content type and complexity effects
Careful dataset curation with 240 real-world videos across 18 themes, rigorous filtering for quality/validity, and complexity scoring along three dimensions (semantic, structural, control)

Strong commitment to reproducibility with detailed implementation details in appendices, clear ethical statement regarding data collection and responsible LLM use, and promise to release prompts, code, and results
weaknesses: Primarily a benchmarking/evaluation contribution rather than advancing generation methods or proposing novel algorithmic solutions; while benchmarking is valuable, this limits impact for top-tier ML conference seeking methodological innovation

Heavy reliance on LLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, DeepSeek-V3) for critical components (complexity scoring, HERD question generation, Content Clarity) with insufficient robustness analysis: no testing across LLM versions, no analysis of hallucination impact, no human validation of LLM-based scoring

Limited validation that proposed metrics correlate with human judgments beyond Section 4.3; Table 5 correlations lack significance tests and confidence intervals; no inter-annotator agreement scores for polarity labeling or complexity scoring

Insufficient actionable insights on how methods should improve: paper documents that methods struggle with temporal consistency and inter-event coherence but provides limited guidance on solutions or mechanistic understanding of failures

Missing critical ablation studies on framework components (which dimensions matter most?), sensitivity to hyperparameters (temporal ordering weight in Eq. 1?), and metric design choices (why 10s clips for DOVER when videos are 40+ seconds?)
Modest dataset scale (240 videos) and lack of analysis on how performance/insights scale with larger datasets; 18 themes may miss long-tail content domains

Insufficient discussion of framework limitations: no analysis of edge cases (intentionally surreal content where inconsistency is artistic), types of videos/prompts that might not be handled well, or cascading errors from tool failures

Statistical rigor concerns: correlation coefficients lack significance testing and multiple-comparison corrections; sample sizes unclear; no confidence intervals; missing details on how missing/unmatched events handled in Hungarian algorithm

HERD metric uses binary yes/no format which oversimplifies nuanced high-level concepts; polarity annotation, while careful, still involves human judgment that could introduce inconsistencies without documented IAA

Limited novelty beyond benchmarking: individual components build on existing work; insights are largely observational rather than prescriptive; no new generation methods proposed that leverage benchmark insights

strengths: Addresses clear gap in existing benchmarks by evaluating long-form videos under complex prompts; prompts substantially more complex (248.85 avg words, 8.70 complexity) than prior work
Comprehensive multi-dimensional evaluation framework with novel contributions including hierarchical Dendriform VQA for fine-grained alignment and HERD metric for narrative-level assessment
Rigorous benchmark construction with multi-stage MLLM-based generation, human verification, and careful handling of consistency, safety, and duplicates

Thorough empirical validation: 13 representative LVG methods evaluated, human alignment study with correlation analysis, diagnostic findings identify specific weaknesses (character consistency ~40%) that motivate future work
Excellent documentation with comprehensive appendices, implementation details, LLM prompts, and qualitative case studies supporting reproducibility
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-structured methodology sections
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: perceptual quality, temporal quality, and dynamic quality primarily adapt existing methods (VBench, DEVIL); main novel contributions are hierarchical VQA and HERD metric

Moderate human alignment for critical dimensions: FGA (SRCC=52.70, PLCC=53.55), Character Consistency (SRCC=49.90), Character Development (SRCC=41.06) suggest metrics may not fully capture human perception, particularly for character-related aspects identified as key weaknesses

HERD metric has inherent subjectivity: expectations are LLM-generated from prompts, introducing systematic bias; 'prompt-centric reference' differs from human-grounded expectations despite dual-agent framework improvements
Complex evaluation pipeline with multiple tool dependencies (SAM3→MLLM→FG-CLIP2 for character consistency) creates error propagation potential with no ablation studies or failure analysis provided

Insufficient justification for key methodological choices: only 100 videos for DQ linear model fitting is very small; specific parameter selections (α, β for PQ sampling) unexplained; low complexity metric variance (2.87%-4.40%) questions utility given weak performance correlations
Modest dataset scale (234 videos) with tightly clustered complexity scores (std. dev. 2-4%) limits ability to test difficulty variations and generalize findings

Background Consistency evaluation questionable: BC computed on full frames outperforms character-masked approach (SRCC 52.80 vs 18.63), contradicting the stated purpose of isolating background stability
Sharp OA-FGA gap (e.g., 45% vs 32% in Table 2) lacks deeper investigation; only surface-level discussion of why models struggle with fine-grained aspects
Heavy reliance on LLMs at multiple stages (generation, verification, evaluation) introduces systematic biases with no analysis of robustness to LLM version changes
Heavy reliance on specific model versions (GPT-5, SAM3, FG-CLIP2) and YouTube videos may limit long-term reproducibility; code/data release timeline not mentioned

strengths: Addresses timely problem: Long-form video generation with complex prompts is a genuine challenge requiring better evaluation frameworks
Comprehensive multi-dimensional framework: Five evaluation dimensions (PQ, TVA, TQ, DQ, HERD) covering 25 sub-dimensions is substantially more complete than existing benchmarks
Well-designed hierarchical fine-grained alignment: The dendriform VQA with gating mechanism (Section 4.2.2) is thoughtfully structured for scene-by-scene evaluation
Significantly more complex prompts: Dataset features 248.85 average words and 8.70 complexity score, substantially exceeding existing benchmarks, with rich hierarchical metadata
Clear diagnostic findings: Stark contrast between high background consistency (>90%) and low character consistency (<40%) provides valuable insights into current model limitations
Human validation effort: Includes human annotation studies and compares alternative HERD implementations, demonstrating care for empirical validation
Extensive benchmarking: Evaluation of 13 representative methods provides broad empirical perspective on current capabilities
weaknesses: Weak human alignment for critical metrics: Table 3 shows concerning SRCC values (FGA: 0.527, Character Consistency: 0.499, Background Consistency w/ removal: 0.308). Only 5% of videos (~12 samples) annotated—insufficient for robust validation

Circular evaluation design: Multiple MLLMs create cascading error potential; Fine-grained and overall alignment both assess same video-text relationships; HERD expectations generated by GPT-5 then evaluated against GPT-5 expectations

Unvalidated scene-level prompt division: Critical preprocessing step (Fig. 7) involving LLM decomposition and manual correction lacks quality validation and could systematically disadvantage certain methods
Limited dataset scale and diversity: 234 videos across only 18 themes is modest for 2026; uneven distribution; all prompts are descriptions of real videos, limiting creative scenario coverage

Weak statistical rigor: No significance testing or confidence intervals; complexity metrics show extremely low variance (Table 7: 2.84–17.76%); weak correlations with complexity (Fig. 11) question metric validity; DQ linear model fitted on only 100 videos

Incremental metric novelty: PQ uses existing DeQA-Score; OA is standard MLLM scoring; FGA builds on existing VQA approaches; TQ reuses established metrics; HERD complexity not justified by superior performance (Fig. 4 shows alternatives are comparable)

HERD metric design issues: Expectations generated without validation against human expectations; dual-agent framework not demonstrably superior (Visual Style performs better with QA-based method); aggregating 1–5 scale as percentages is unconventional
Overly ambitious scope: 8-page main paper with 30+ page appendix; critical details relegated to appendix; lacks depth in failure-mode analysis or ablation studies

Missing methodological justification: Large OA-FGA gap (40–55 vs. 10–45) suggests these measure different constructs—implications not discussed; character removal for BC validated post-hoc rather than by design; scene division error effects on method rankings unquantified

Reproducibility concerns: Heavy dependence on proprietary models and specific versions (GPT-5, Seed1.5-VL); unclear if hierarchical metadata will be released; generation at 480p may be suboptimal for some methods

strengths: Addresses clear gap in long-form, complex text-to-video evaluation with 234 high-quality videos and significantly longer, more complex prompts (248.85 words, 8.70 complexity score) than existing benchmarks

Comprehensive multi-dimensional evaluation framework with novel components: fine-grained alignment via hierarchical VQA, HERD metric for narrative aspects, and streaming implementations for scalability
Rigorous dataset construction with multi-stage MLLM-based curation plus human verification; empirical validation through human alignment studies showing reasonable correlations (SRCC 40-70% range)
Well-structured evaluation revealing actionable insights: current methods show strong perceptual quality but critical weaknesses in fine-grained alignment and character consistency
Extensive benchmarking of 13 diverse LVG methods with detailed appendices, implementation details, and case studies supporting reproducibility and community use
weaknesses: Dataset size (234 videos) is relatively modest for benchmark intended to drive long-term research; all videos from YouTube in English, limiting domain/language generalization; no analysis of coverage gaps across 18 themes
Heavy dependence on proprietary/complex models (GPT-5, Seed1.5-VL, SAM3, multiple CLIPs) creates reproducibility concerns and uncertain long-term maintainability; quality bounds are unclear

Fair comparison compromised: scene-level prompt division for multi-prompt methods may introduce bias; different methods require different settings (SkyReels-V2, Vlogger, VGoT don't work at 480p)—impact unanalyzed

Metric validation concerns: (1) complexity metric shows low variance (2-4%) and weak correlation with performance, questioning utility; (2) HERD sub-dimensions show moderate human alignment (Character Development 42.70% PLCC); (3) FGA entirely depends on LLM-generated questions without validation of coverage adequacy

Incomplete analytical framework: no ablations on which dimensions matter most, missing error analysis, no inter-rater agreement reported, Dynamic Quality aggregation uses linear model fitted on only 100 videos, no significance testing
HERD dual-agent framework admits potential hallucinations (acknowledged for Visual Style in Fig. 4) but doesn't quantify frequency/impact; unclear robustness across diverse video types
